topic: machine0: Persistent CPU and GPU VMs from the CLI
summary: machine0 (YC S26, founder Barnaby Malet) sells persistent KVM/QEMU virtual machines driven from a CLI (every command has --json) or a remote MCP server. It targets long-horizon agents: a coding agent that runs 6-8 hours, an RL/auto-research loop that runs for days, or 24/7 agent fleets. VMs stay on until stopped/suspended/destroyed, get dedicated (non-shared) CPU/RAM, a static public IP and HTTPS at <vm>.mac0.io, across 5 regions at identical per-minute prices. Differentiators vs the sandbox crowd: it is a persistent computer rather than an ephemeral code runner, it offers real GPUs up to 8x H200, and it can suspend (disk snapshot, compute billing stops) and snapshot/clone golden images.

key_points: Authoritative pricing (per-minute, same price in every region). CPU floor: small 1 vCPU/1 GB/25 GB at $0.013/hr (~$9/mo); top CPU tier 6xl 60 vCPU/240 GB/900 GB at $3.714/hr (~$2,711/mo).
Two CPU variants: '-nvme' (newer-gen CPUs + NVMe for higher disk IOPS at same vCPU/RAM/disk) and '-premium' (dedicated, not shared, vCPUs - their fastest single-thread tier).
Suspended VMs bill only image storage at $0.078/GB/month; persistent disks ~$0.1667/GB/month; $5 minimum top-up, unused credits refundable.
5 regions: us-east (New York), us-west (San Francisco), uk (London), eu (Amsterdam), asia (Singapore). GPU sizes are offered in us-east, uk, eu and asia - not us-west.
Founder framing: the pain is that agent workloads moved from ephemeral to always-on - coding agents run 6-8 hours, auto-research agents run for days, OpenClaw and Hermes run 24/7.

The four named pain points are Resources (a few agents saturate RAM/CPU), Security ('--yolo' on your laptop is one prompt injection away from exfiltrated credentials), Availability (close the laptop and the agent dies mid-task) and Isolation.

Profiles bundle MCP connections, credentials, prompts and env vars and inject them at VM creation so each agent gets exactly the capabilities you choose and nothing else; the VM's Claude Code/Codex pick them up automatically on SSH.
Explicit positioning: 'One command spins up a persistent VM. Your agent drives it via CLI or MCP, building its own fleet from 1 vCPU up to 60 vCPU / 240 GB and 8xH100s.'
Launch HN thread (Launch HN: machine0, YC S26) - the main skeptical/technical Q&A and the source of most caveats.
Founder: it runs on top of DigitalOcean infrastructure; BYOC is on the roadmap; 'we're not the cheapest compute on the market, but cheaper than most sandbox providers/neoclouds'.

Suspend semantics clarified: NO CRIU - 'Snapshots are at the disk layer, not RAM... so processes restart, they don't resume mid-execution. Practically: anything that survives a reboot survives a suspend.'
Stopped (not suspended) VMs bill at full rate - you must suspend to stop compute billing.

Credential rotation is the open edge: founder says OAuth refresh is handled inside the profile and re-inject is possible, but a commenter (bobbylarson) pressed that a process holding a credential read at boot keeps the stale value in memory - revocation mid-session is 'not solved cleanly without short TTLs'.

Moats questioned: commenters argued the minimal API is not defensible ('could be vibecoded as a pile of scripts', vendor lock-in), and that AWS/GCP/Hetzner/DigitalOcean APIs are already agent-orchestrable - the founder's answer is simpler grammar (new, ls, rm) saving context/turns and avoiding orphaned artifacts (security groups, volumes, elastic IPs).

fly.io Sprites comparison: founder claims advantage is GPUs, much bigger machines, full VM control down to drivers/kernel, cheaper for compute-intensive workloads, plus profile-based MCP/credential injection and NixOS.
Pricing-transparency criticism: 'from $0.013/hr' without the full table drew pushback ("It ranges from cold to orange!").
NixOS image shipped on an EOL release (25.11) at launch - founder acknowledged and said he would republish base images.
Independent hands-on comparison of 7 agent-compute products (docs, pricing pages and SDKs reviewed; prices as of Sep 26, 2026).
Lifetime is the first cut: machine0 and Fly.io Sprites persist indefinitely; OpenComputer v2 caps at a hard 8 hours; E2B, Vercel Sandbox and Modal cap a continuous session at 24 hours on paid plans.
Isolation is not uniform: machine0 and OpenComputer run full KVM VMs; E2B, Vercel and Sprites use Firecracker microVMs; Modal uses gVisor; Daytona defaults to Linux containers.
Cost for a 2 vCPU / 4 GB machine running flat out for one hour: machine0 $0.052, E2B and Daytona $0.166, Modal $0.238, OpenComputer $0.378 - machine0 is ~3x cheaper than E2B/Daytona at that shape.

Key tradeoff stated plainly: 'machine0 bills while stopped, though, and the usage-billed ones cost far less when the agent is mostly waiting on a model' - i.e. machine0 wins for always-on work, loses for bursty tool-call workloads.
Five dimensions separate the platforms: cold start, isolation, session persistence, SDK ergonomics and pricing - and no platform wins all five.

Measured cold starts: Daytona 742 ms create, E2B 717 ms, Vercel 1852 ms, Modal 2437 ms, Blaxel 2824 ms. machine0 does not compete on cold start - it is a persistent VM (cold-boot from disk on start), not a millisecond tool-call runner.
Persistence is not one thing: E2B pauses with memory intact, Daytona only on VM sandboxes, the rest save the filesystem - matching machine0's documented disk-level suspend.
Pricing models split three ways: per-second full duration (E2B, Daytona), per-second active with scale-to-zero (Modal, Vercel active-CPU), and machine0's per-minute always-on-until-suspended.
GPU support is a filter: E2B and Blaxel list no GPU, which removes them for training/fine-tuning workloads where machine0 is competitive.
23-platform landscape survey (updated Sep 16, 2026) - useful for placing machine0 in the wider market.
Central caveat for any such review: 'Does persistence mean a running process resumes? Not necessarily. Some products preserve only files, while others retain memory in specific pause modes.'

A VM boundary, an egress policy and scoped credentials solve three different problems and must be verified separately - a microVM isolates guest execution from the host but does not stop exfiltration through allowed network destinations or granted credentials.
Idle-compute savings do not eliminate storage, subscription, inference or operational costs - directly relevant to machine0's stopped-VM and storage billing.
Runtime class is becoming explicit across vendors (Daytona container/VM/GPU classes, Modal VM Sandboxes beta and CPU-only), so 'which isolation' is now a per-workload decision.

Vendor-authored but useful taxonomy: agents buy one of three product shapes - a stateless code runner, a persistent computer, or a control plane managing fleets of either. machine0 is squarely a persistent computer.
Most bad picks come from buying the wrong shape: 'Pick by feature list and you find out in week three that your coding agent's working tree evaporated at the ten-minute mark.'

Stateless runners have short default ceilings (Modal Sandbox ~5 min default lifetime; Cloudflare deletes files and processes when the container stops) - the contrast that makes machine0's persistence the headline feature.

Confirms the crowded competitive field machine0 must explain itself against: E2B, Modal, Daytona, Vercel Sandbox, Cloudflare Sandbox and Fly.io Sprites all use the word 'sandbox' for different boundaries.

stats.fact: machine0 CPU VM floor is 1 vCPU / 1 GB / 25 GB disk at $0.013/hr (~$9/month), billed per minute with no commitment.
Largest CPU tier is 60 vCPU / 240 GB RAM / 900 GB disk at $3.714/hr (~$2,711/month).
GPU VMs start at $0.836/hr (1x RTX 4000 Ada) and scale to 8x H200 at $39.336/hr with 1,128 GB total VRAM.
Suspended VMs stop compute billing and pay only image storage at $0.078/GB/month; persistent disks cost ~$0.1667/GB/month.
machine0 quotes a 99.99% VM-level uptime SLA across 5 regions at identical per-minute pricing.
For a 2 vCPU / 4 GB machine running one hour flat out, machine0 costs $0.052 vs E2B and Daytona $0.166, Modal $0.238, OpenComputer $0.378.
Stopped-but-not-suspended VMs bill at full rate - cloud resources remain reserved, so only suspend or destroy stops the meter.
Suspend is a disk-layer snapshot, not CRIU: processes restart on 'machine0 start', they do not resume mid-execution.
Every VM is a full KVM/QEMU virtual machine (not a container or gVisor sandbox) with kernel-level access and the real GPU driver exposed to the guest.
machine0 runs on DigitalOcean infrastructure; BYOC (bring your own cloud) is roadmap, not shipped.
The ubuntu-24-04-loaded image ships Docker, Node.js, Python, Go, Rust, Bun, Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, tmux, zoxide, fzf, ripgrep and bat pre-installed.
Persistence benchmark: machine0 and Fly.io Sprites persist indefinitely, OpenComputer v2 caps at 8 hours, and E2B/Vercel/Modal cap continuous sessions at 24 hours on paid plans.
Cold-start leaders are E2B (~717 ms) and Daytona (~742 ms) vs Modal (~2437 ms) - machine0 competes on persistence and GPU depth, not millisecond startup.
Security defaults: SSH-only with password auth disabled, root login disabled, ufw enabled with ports 22/80/443 open, private keys never leave the user's machine.

angles: The real question is not 'is it a good VM' but 'do you want a sandbox or a computer' - machine0 bets that always-on agents (6-8h coding runs, multi-day RL/auto-research loops, 24/7 OpenClaw/Hermes fleets) need a persistent machine, while E2B/Modal/Daytona optimize the opposite tradeoff.
Suspend is disk-level, not memory-level (no CRIU): anything that survives a reboot survives a suspend - set expectations that this is not mid-execution process resumption.
The billing trap that costs real money: stopped VMs bill at full rate. Suspend or destroy. Auto-topup is on by default once a card is saved.

Cost crossover analysis: machine0 is ~3x cheaper per hour than E2B/Daytona at 2 vCPU/4 GB, but the usage-billed rivals cost far less when the agent is mostly waiting on a model - the break-even is roughly 'is your agent busy or idle?'

Profiles as the genuinely agent-native feature: injecting MCP servers, credentials, prompts and env vars at VM creation is what makes a fleet of agents manageable - but credential revocation mid-session remains unsolved without short TTLs.

GPU depth versus sandbox rivals: E2B and Blaxel offer no GPU, so training, fine-tuning and RL workloads have almost no choice among the agent-sandbox category - machine0 goes to 8x H200 with 1,128 GB VRAM on a single box.

Vendor-skeptic angle: the minimal CLI is not a moat (DigitalOcean already has an MCP, and the founder admits it is not the cheapest compute) - the honest case for machine0 is DX plus the product mix, not exclusivity.
Pricing transparency: marketing leads with 'from $0.013/hr' but the top CPU tier is ~285x that price - read the full size table before committing.

NixOS-first reproducible machines: declarative flakes, deterministic builds and one-command rollbacks make the environment itself portable and version-controlled - the counter-argument to suspend-and-pray state preservation.
